If you show up, work hard, pay what you owe—taxes, rent, time—then you should get the basics back: safe streets, decent schools, a clinic that sees you without making you feel small. Fairness also means the rules aren’t a moving target. Don’t tell people to “get in line” if the line is ten years long and changes every year. And it’s not fair when bosses pay cash to dodge minimum wage, then call ICE when workers ask for what they earned. I still remember helping a friend who cleaned offices—she was shorted two weeks’ pay and too scared to press it. We passed a hat at church and got her groceries, but that’s not fairness. That’s a bandage.

Belonging is being seen without having to shrink yourself. It’s hearing your name said right and not being laughed at for your lunch. It’s being able to switch to Spanish with your tia outside the store without getting side-eye. When my daughter’s teacher learned a few phrases to talk to my mom at conferences, my mom’s whole face lit up—she finally felt like part of the school, not just a visitor. Belonging is also about safety: not waking up wondering if a raid will sweep through the neighborhood; being able to get a driver’s license so you’re not one taillight away from your life falling apart. When people don’t have to hide, they can join—PTA, soccer, block cleanups. That’s how belonging grows.

Community is the everyday promises we keep to each other. We watch each other’s kids when shifts run late. We trade rides, share casseroles, pass along a stroller when a new baby shows up next door. We check on the older neighbor when his porch light stays off. We also set boundaries—noise down after 10, pick up after your dog, keep the stairs clear—because respect is part of community too. At our community garden, we’ve got folks from everywhere—English, Spanish, a little Mixtec—arguing about tomatoes and then splitting the harvest anyway. When there’s hurt—like our neighbor who struggles with drinking—we don’t pretend it isn’t there. We knock, we bring soup, we offer numbers for help, and we keep the block safe. Not perfect. Just present.

What stands out most in my life are small moments that taught me all three at once. My dad being told to “go back” even though he wore steel-toe boots six days a week and could quote the union contract by heart. My cousin finally getting her papers and crying because she could sign her real name at the clinic. The time a store manager told a cashier to stop speaking Spanish to an elderly customer, and a line of us stepped in—politely, firmly—and the manager backed off. Fairness, belonging, community—they’re not slogans to me. They’re those tiny decisions we make every day to treat each other like we matter.

I try to meet that with patience: a few words in Spanish or English, a hand gesture, a laugh, and we figure it out. If I can translate, I do. If I can’t, I slow down and smile. When we work a bed side by side, it reminds me that community isn’t about being the same; it’s about showing up, giving each other room, and keeping our promises.

People are carrying all kinds of things—joy, grief, habits they’re trying to quit, faith that looks different from mine, love that doesn’t match someone else’s picture. If we lead with respect and make the rules about behavior, not identity, most folks relax.

What helps everyone feel comfortable, in my experience:
- Start with names and small kindnesses. Learn how to say someone’s name, offer a spare trowel, share extra herbs. That breaks the ice without putting people on the spot.
- Clear, simple ground rules that apply to everyone: no using drugs or drinking in shared spaces, keep noise down after a certain hour, clean up your plot and the path, be kind to kids and elders, no harassment—about language, religion, race, who someone loves, or anything else.
- Privacy and consent. We don’t pry about health or papers. If someone shares, we keep it in confidence. We ask before taking photos.
- Language bridges. Post signs in English and Spanish (and more if needed), keep a list of volunteer translators, and be patient with pauses. A smile and a gesture go a long way.
- Safety without shame. For neighbors dealing with addiction, we keep the space drug- and alcohol-free, but we don’t humiliate anyone. We offer water, a seat, a ride to a clinic or a meeting if they want it, and we have phone numbers for outreach teams. If there’s a real safety issue, we step in as a group and, if needed, call for help.
- Basic health sense for everyone. Handwashing station, gloves in the shed, a first-aid kit. We treat cuts, clean tools, and don’t share personal items. And we remember most illnesses don’t spread through casual contact, so there’s no reason to isolate or stigmatize anyone.
- Honor people’s families as they are. Married, not married, two moms, two dads, single parent, roommates—if the kids are safe and the adults are respectful, they’re welcome. We focus on how folks act, not how their household is arranged.
- Make room for faith and culture without letting it trample others. You can pray quietly on a bench; you can also play music at a reasonable volume. We rotate potluck menus, swap recipes, and keep jokes away from anyone’s ethnicity, accent, or beliefs.

Where we need more communication and extra tolerance:
- Addiction and mental health. Some neighbors see it as “bad choices,” others as illness. I’ve learned it’s both complicated and human. Talking about boundaries—what’s okay here, what’s not—and sharing resources helps. The reason is simple: shame doesn’t heal anyone, but loose boundaries don’t keep kids safe. We need both compassion and lines.
- Health fears. People get scared around words like “infectious,” sometimes because of old myths. A little straight talk—how things are and aren’t spread, that gloves and handwashing protect everyone—calms nerves. The reason is fear fills silence; facts and routines take its place.
- Religion and LGBTQ+ neighbors. Some of our older folks or church folks (and I’ve got church folks in my family) need to hear that greeting a same-sex couple or using someone’s pronouns isn’t “agreeing” with anything—it’s basic manners. - Language and pace. Not everyone moves on “U.S. time” or argues the same way. We say what we need—“Let’s start at 6 sharp,” “One person speaks at a time,” “Keep it to two minutes”—and we enforce it gently. The reason: structure lets different styles fit together without anyone feeling steamrolled.
- Race and class tension. Sometimes folks blame “new people” for crowded schools or jobs getting thin. I try to pull the lens back: most of us are squeezed by the same rents and wages. We ask for better from the city, instead of fighting over crumbs. The reason: punching sideways doesn’t fix what’s broken.

Under it all, I try to stick to this: call people in before you call them out, unless someone’s in danger. Address behavior, not who someone is. Offer a next step—“Here’s a trash bag,” “Here’s a number,” “Let’s set a time to talk”—not just a scold. And remember, comfort isn’t the same as safety. We won’t all be comfortable all the time in a mixed neighborhood. But if folks know the space is fair and they won’t be shamed for showing up as themselves—and that there are real consequences for crossing lines—that’s when a garden turns into a community.

Belonging is being seen without having to shrink yourself. It’s hearing your name said right and not being laughed at for your lunch. It’s being able to switch to Spanish with your tia outside the store without getting side-eye. When my daughter’s teacher learned a few phrases to talk to my mom at conferences, my mom’s whole face lit up—she finally felt like part of the school, not just a visitor. Belonging is also about safety: not waking up wondering if a raid will sweep through the neighborhood; being able to get a driver’s license so you’re not one taillight away from your life falling apart. When people don’t have to hide, they can join—PTA, soccer, block cleanups. That’s how belonging grows.

Community is the everyday promises we keep to each other. We watch each other’s kids when shifts run late. We trade rides, share casseroles, pass along a stroller when a new baby shows up next door. We check on the older neighbor when his porch light stays off. We also set boundaries—noise down after 10, pick up after your dog, keep the stairs clear—because respect is part of community too. At our community garden, we’ve got folks from everywhere—English, Spanish, a little Mixtec—arguing about tomatoes and then splitting the harvest anyway. When there’s hurt—like our neighbor who struggles with drinking—we don’t pretend it isn’t there. We knock, we bring soup, we offer numbers for help, and we keep the block safe. Not perfect. Just present.

What stands out most in my life are small moments that taught me all three at once. My dad being told to “go back” even though he wore steel-toe boots six days a week and could quote the union contract by heart. My cousin finally getting her papers and crying because she could sign her real name at the clinic. The time a store manager told a cashier to stop speaking Spanish to an elderly customer, and a line of us stepped in—politely, firmly—and the manager backed off. Fairness, belonging, community—they’re not slogans to me. They’re those tiny decisions we make every day to treat each other like we matter.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character17_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting in the garden, I mostly feel curious and open. I grew up straddling worlds—Spanish at home, English at school and work—so mixed spaces don’t scare me. I like learning folks’ names, how to say them right, and asking about their plants before anything heavier. You can learn a lot about a person from how they water a bed or share extra seedlings. Food and flowers make it easier—someone brings cilantro starts, someone else shares mint, and next thing you know we’re swapping recipes and stories about our moms.

I’m comfortable around difference because our block has always been a mix—new arrivals, old-timers, families like mine, folks who look nothing like me. What matters to me is respect: say hello, make eye contact, keep the path clear, turn the music down after a certain hour, and don’t make fun of someone’s accent or headscarf or who they hold hands with. I don’t need everyone to think like me; I need us to look out for one another’s kids and keep the space clean.

There are awkward moments—language gaps, different ideas of “on time,” someone not sure of the unspoken rules. I try to meet that with patience: a few words in Spanish or English, a hand gesture, a laugh, and we figure it out. If I can translate, I do. If I can’t, I slow down and smile. I’ve learned to start small: share tomatoes, trade tools, then talk about bigger things once there’s trust.

I’ll be honest: sometimes I’m tired. Long shifts, bills due, and then you come home and there’s a new set of neighbors and new norms to learn. But most days, choosing to engage pays off. The garden is where I remember we’re all carrying something—homesickness, pride, stress, hope. When we work a bed side by side, it reminds me that community isn’t about being the same; it’s about showing up, giving each other room, and keeping our promises.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
In the garden, I try to keep two things front and center: dignity and boundaries. People are carrying all kinds of things—joy, grief, habits they’re trying to quit, faith that looks different from mine, love that doesn’t match someone else’s picture. If we lead with respect and make the rules about behavior, not identity, most folks relax.

What helps everyone feel comfortable, in my experience:
- Start with names and small kindnesses. Learn how to say someone’s name, offer a spare trowel, share extra herbs. That breaks the ice without putting people on the spot.
- Clear, simple ground rules that apply to everyone: no using drugs or drinking in shared spaces, keep noise down after a certain hour, clean up your plot and the path, be kind to kids and elders, no harassment—about language, religion, race, who someone loves, or anything else.
- Privacy and consent. We don’t pry about health or papers. If someone shares, we keep it in confidence. We ask before taking photos.
- Language bridges. Post signs in English and Spanish (and more if needed), keep a list of volunteer translators, and be patient with pauses. A smile and a gesture go a long way.
- Safety without shame. For neighbors dealing with addiction, we keep the space drug- and alcohol-free, but we don’t humiliate anyone. We offer water, a seat, a ride to a clinic or a meeting if they want it, and we have phone numbers for outreach teams. If there’s a real safety issue, we step in as a group and, if needed, call for help.
- Basic health sense for everyone. Handwashing station, gloves in the shed, a first-aid kit. We treat cuts, clean tools, and don’t share personal items. And we remember most illnesses don’t spread through casual contact, so there’s no reason to isolate or stigmatize anyone.
- Honor people’s families as they are. Married, not married, two moms, two dads, single parent, roommates—if the kids are safe and the adults are respectful, they’re welcome. We focus on how folks act, not how their household is arranged.
- Make room for faith and culture without letting it trample others. You can pray quietly on a bench; you can also play music at a reasonable volume. We rotate potluck menus, swap recipes, and keep jokes away from anyone’s ethnicity, accent, or beliefs.

Where we need more communication and extra tolerance:
- Addiction and mental health. Some neighbors see it as “bad choices,” others as illness. I’ve learned it’s both complicated and human. Talking about boundaries—what’s okay here, what’s not—and sharing resources helps. The reason is simple: shame doesn’t heal anyone, but loose boundaries don’t keep kids safe. We need both compassion and lines.
- Health fears. People get scared around words like “infectious,” sometimes because of old myths. A little straight talk—how things are and aren’t spread, that gloves and handwashing protect everyone—calms nerves. The reason is fear fills silence; facts and routines take its place.
- Religion and LGBTQ+ neighbors. Some of our older folks or church folks (and I’ve got church folks in my family) need to hear that greeting a same-sex couple or using someone’s pronouns isn’t “agreeing” with anything—it’s basic manners. The reason: you can hold your beliefs and still treat people the way you want to be treated.
- Language and pace. Not everyone moves on “U.S. time” or argues the same way. We say what we need—“Let’s start at 6 sharp,” “One person speaks at a time,” “Keep it to two minutes”—and we enforce it gently. The reason: structure lets different styles fit together without anyone feeling steamrolled.
- Race and class tension. Sometimes folks blame “new people” for crowded schools or jobs getting thin. I try to pull the lens back: most of us are squeezed by the same rents and wages. We ask for better from the city, instead of fighting over crumbs. The reason: punching sideways doesn’t fix what’s broken.

Under it all, I try to stick to this: call people in before you call them out, unless someone’s in danger. Address behavior, not who someone is. Offer a next step—“Here’s a trash bag,” “Here’s a number,” “Let’s set a time to talk”—not just a scold. And remember, comfort isn’t the same as safety. We won’t all be comfortable all the time in a mixed neighborhood. But if folks know the space is fair and they won’t be shamed for showing up as themselves—and that there are real consequences for crossing lines—that’s when a garden turns into a community.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character17_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs get thin, fairness to me means two things at once: nobody gets treated like they’re disposable, and nobody gets to win by breaking the rules. I don’t blame the man who crosses a border to feed his kids any more than I blame the woman down the block working two shifts. I blame the setup that lets bosses play us against each other—hire off the books, underpay, then shrug when the neighborhood turns on itself.

What balance looks like, from where I sit:

- One wage floor, real enforcement. Equal pay for equal work, no matter where you were born or what papers you have. Make wage theft and misclassification hurt—fines, back pay, no more city contracts for violators. When everyone has to follow the same labor laws, the undercutting slows down.

- Local first on public money. If the city or state is paying—road work, school kitchens, hospital cleaning—give locals a first shot: a hiring window, apprenticeships, union pathways. Pair that with real training and childcare so people can actually take the jobs.

- Tell the truth about “shortages.” If a company says “we can’t find workers,” show the wage. If it’s $11 and no benefits, raise it before importing a crew. If it’s still empty at a fair wage, then bring in workers with protections.

- Clean, fair work permits tied to real needs. For sectors that truly need more hands—ag, elder care, some trades—use visas that demand living wages, safe housing where relevant, no recruitment fees, and the right to change employers. Don’t trap people with one boss; that’s how abuse happens.

- Bring longtime neighbors into the light. Folks who’ve been here for years, paying taxes with ITINs, no serious crimes—give them a way to get right. It’s better for everyone when people can report bad bosses, get licensed, and compete fairly.

- Invest where newcomers land. Schools need ESL teachers, clinics need interpreters, buses need more runs. Fund that so it’s not just the same classrooms and waiting rooms taking on more with less.

- Stop the temp churn. I’ve watched warehouses cut hours for regulars, then bring in a cheaper temp crew. Make employers offer extra hours to current workers before hiring new ones, and hold big firms responsible for what their contractors do.

- Back small businesses to do right. A lot of mom-and-pop shops want to follow the rules but feel squeezed. Help with compliance, grants to raise wages, and clear, simple paperwork lowers the temptation to go cash-only.

- Worker voice across lines. Support organizing and hotlines in multiple languages. If people can stand together without fear of retaliation or deportation, the floor rises for everyone.

- Adjust by data, not panic. If unemployment spikes in a region or sector, slow new hiring from outside there and pour money into training. If there’s a real gap—say, welders or home health aides—open up, but with standards.

Why I feel this way: I’ve seen how scarcity makes neighbors suspicious. My cousin in housekeeping lost hours when the hotel subcontracted; the new crew got paid less and people started blaming “them.” But when we pushed for the same wage and benefits for everyone on site, the tension cooled. It wasn’t the workers; it was the loophole.

Fairness isn’t closing the door. It’s closing the trapdoors—those little drop floors where some folks fall through and drag the rest of us down with them. If we set one clear set of rules, lift wages, and share the ladders—training, childcare, language classes—locals and migrants stop being rivals and go back to being co-workers and neighbors. That’s the balance I can live with.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character17_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
When I hear all those views, I sort them into three buckets: what I see with my own eyes, what makes sense if we fix the rules, and what needs facts so we don’t let fear run the show.

What feels true to me:
- Immigrants fill real gaps. In my world it’s kitchens, caregiving, construction, warehouses. When the work is hard, hours are long, and pay is thin, newcomers often step in. That’s not a bad thing; it’s how families survive.
- Diversity brings life. New groceries on the corner, bilingual signs at the clinic, kids learning each other’s songs—those are wins. Culture makes neighborhoods feel awake, not just crowded.
- People want safety. My neighbors—born here or not—want safe buses, schools, parks. Background checks, clear rules, and consequences for serious crimes are reasonable. Safety should be about behavior, not birthplace.

Where I say, “let’s fix the setup”:
- If there’s a “shortage,” show the wage and conditions. Many “shortages” shrink when pay rises and schedules get humane. If jobs still sit empty, then bring workers with protections.
- Enforce labor laws for everyone. Equal pay for equal work, real penalties for wage theft and under-the-table games. When bosses can’t exploit one group, the race-to-the-bottom slows.
- Invest where people land. ESL teachers, interpreters at clinics, more bus runs, job training with childcare. Integration isn’t magic; it’s work we can plan for.
- Let longtime neighbors get right. Folks here for years, paying taxes, no serious crimes—give them a path. It helps them stand up to bad employers and join the community fully.

What needs facts and steady talk:
- Crime and terrorism fears. I get the instinct to worry, but most research shows immigrants aren’t more likely to commit crimes than people born here. Terrorism tied to new arrivals is rare. We should keep vetting strong, yes, and build trust so people report crimes without fearing immigration fallout.
- “They’re taking our jobs.” Sometimes it feels that way, especially in low-wage work. But the bigger culprits are weak unions, temp subcontracting, automation, and companies dodging standards. Let’s look at local data: wages, hours, hiring practices—then fix what’s actually broken.
- Wage impacts. There can be small dips for workers with similar skills when the floor is weak. Raising the floor—minimum wage, enforcement, organizing—does more to protect incomes than shutting doors.
- Public services strain. Schools and clinics feel the squeeze if funding doesn’t follow population. The answer is fair funding, not blaming families who show up.

Humanitarian piece:
- Refugees and asylum seekers deserve due process and a safe, orderly path. My family knows what it is to flee danger and start over. America’s promise means we don’t turn that into a coin toss. Set numbers we can support, fund resettlement, and help folks get on their feet fast.

How I’d keep the conversation:
- Bring receipts, not rumors. Local stats on wages, vacancies, school enrollment. Plain language, multiple languages.
- Separate people from policies. Don’t scapegoat families; question the systems that keep wages low or leave classrooms underfunded.
- Listen across lines. Union halls, churches, PTA meetings—let workers, newcomers, and old-timers talk about what they’re seeing and what would help.
- Adjust by region. What’s true in a farm county isn’t the same as a shipyard city. Use data to tune visa numbers and training dollars.

In the end, I think most viewpoints come from real feelings—wanting work, safety, and dignity. The parts I co-sign right away: immigrants do vital work, culture enriches us, and refugees deserve a fair shot. The parts that need proof and care: crime and terrorism claims, and the idea that closing doors fixes paychecks. If we make the rules fair and enforce them—one wage floor, strong protections, smart investments—people stop being opponents and go back to being neighbors. That’s the America I still believe in.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character17_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I’m not for swinging the door wide open with no plan, and I’m not for slamming it shut. The sweet spot, for me, is firm but fair: clear lanes to come, honest numbers we can support, and strong worker protections so nobody wins by breaking the rules.

What I’d choose is a mix:
- Job‑demand lanes, with a real wage test. If an employer wants to bring workers, they have to post the wage and prove they tried at a fair rate with decent hours. If the job still sits empty, okay—bring people in. Tie visas to the occupation, not a single boss, so workers can switch employers and avoid abuse.
- Numerical limits that breathe. Set annual ceilings by sector and region, then adjust quarterly based on data—unemployment, vacancies, wage trends. Keep guaranteed slots for refugees and for family reunification, because we’re human beings, not just headcounts.
- An earned path for longtime neighbors. Folks here for years, with clean records, paying taxes—give them a way to regularize. Background checks, fees spread out, English/civics classes. When people are “in the system,” it’s better for wages, safety, and trust.
- One wage floor, enforced for everyone. Equal pay for equal work—no under‑the‑table games, no recruitment fees, no “contractor” labels to dodge benefits. Make wage theft sting: back pay, fines, loss of contracts.
- Integration money that turns on automatically. If arrivals rise, school districts get ESL funding, clinics get interpreters, buses add runs. Don’t ask the same crowded classrooms to do more with nothing.
- Local first on public projects. For city and state contracts, offer locals a hiring window and apprenticeships. Pair that with training, childcare, and language classes so people can actually take the jobs.
- Fast, fair processing at the border. Quick decisions for asylum with case management instead of cages. Return those who don’t qualify safely; help those who do settle fast—IDs, work permits, housing help.
- Transparency and community voice. Publish the data—wages, shortages, visa numbers—in plain language. Let unions, small businesses, churches, and immigrant groups advise on adjustments.

Why not “complete openness”? Because capacity matters. Bus seats, clinic hours, classroom desks—those are real. If we ignore pacing, we just feed backlash and burnout. We need order, not chaos.

Why not “refuse entry”? That’s not who we are, and it doesn’t fit our economy. Agriculture, elder care, some trades—those sectors depend on newcomers. A hard ban would hurt families here and the work that keeps the lights on.

Why not only “job demand”? On its own, it can be gamed. If the wage test is weak, companies cry “shortage” to keep pay low. That’s why I pair it with enforcement, portability, and a living‑wage requirement.

Why not only “numerical limits”? Caps without context are blunt. They ignore local conditions and humanitarian needs. Numbers should flex with data and keep space for refugees and families.

This mix balances fairness and belonging:
- Fairness, because the rules stop moving—clear paths to come, to work, to get right if you’ve been here, and consequences for bosses who cheat.
- Belonging, because we fund the places where people land—schools, clinics, transit—so neighbors don’t feel abandoned.
- Community, because workers stand on the same floor. When nobody can be exploited to undercut the rest, tension drops and folks go back to being co‑workers instead of rivals.

From my life, the lesson is simple: scarcity makes people point fingers sideways. Strong, honest rules turn that energy upward—toward fixing wages, funding classrooms, and holding bad actors to account. Let people in through doors we can hold open, at a pace we can carry, and treat every pair of hands with the same dignity. That’s a policy I can defend at the garden gate and at the union hall.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character17_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character17_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Stepping in as her brought back how grounded her politics were. She didn’t start with big theories; she started with lunchboxes, late shifts, parent‑teacher nights, and the block. A few things crystallized for me:

- She separated safety from comfort. Safety was non‑negotiable, tied to behavior and clear boundaries. Comfort was shared and imperfect in a mixed community—something you work at with courtesy, not something you enforce on others’ identities.

- Fairness, to her, meant predictable rules plus enforcement. Not just “be fair,” but “make wage theft sting, make visas portable, stop moving the goalposts.” That emphasis on closing loopholes more than closing doors landed differently this time.

- Belonging sounded less like speeches and more like infrastructure: ESL teachers, interpreters at clinics, bus routes that actually run, IDs and work permits processed on time. She treated integration as logistics, not magic.

- She was skeptical of the word “shortage” without the wage next to it. If pay and conditions are bad, of course there’s a shortage. Fix those first; then fill real gaps with protections.

- Her “call people in before you call them out” line had teeth only because it sat next to clear consequences. Compassion and boundaries, both.

For my own views, I notice some shifts:
- I used to frame immigration mostly as a border question. After speaking as her, I see labor standards and enforcement as the real pressure valve. If everyone stands on the same floor, a lot of the heat goes out of the room.

- I’m more open to “breathing” numerical limits tied to data, paired with strong job‑demand lanes that can’t be gamed. Before, I leaned on caps as a blunt tool; now I think the flex and transparency matter more than the raw number.

- I’m firmer on an earned path for long‑time neighbors. I saw it in her stories: bringing people into the light helps wages, safety, and trust.

- I’m less tempted to blame newcomers for local strain and more focused on whether funding follows population. If we don’t resource schools and clinics, we set neighbors up to fight over scraps.

What surprised me most was how consistent she was: behavior, not identity; data over panic; doors we can hold open, not swing or slam. Saying it out loud made me miss her, but it also made her way of problem‑solving feel usable—something I can carry into how I talk about this with family, at church, or at work.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character17_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll answer as Character17_F.

You know, for me, "fairness" is about everyone having a real shot—like, not just in words, but in practice. Growing up in a lower-income Hispanic family, I saw how folks work twice as hard just to get half as much. So fairness isn’t just about rules, it’s about looking at who actually gets left out and finding ways to lift them up. It bugs me when people say "life’s fair if you work hard," because I’ve watched my own parents break their backs and still get ignored or pushed to the margins.

Belonging is harder. In some places, I’ve always felt like I was "other," even when it’s my own neighborhood. Sometimes just the way people look at you or talk over you makes you feel invisible. But I also know the warmth of real community—like Sunday cookouts or church events, where everyone brings something and you don’t have to pretend to be anything you’re not. That sense of belonging is precious, but it takes work from everyone. You have to let people in, and not just the ones who look or sound like you.

When I think of "community," to me it means standing up for each other, even if we’re different. If someone’s struggling—like losing a job or dealing with immigration stuff—we help, not judge. My mom always said, "We all eat, or nobody eats." That’s the kind of community I try to build: not just friendly faces, but people who show up. I’ve seen what happens when folks get divided, when rumors spread about "newcomers" or "outsiders." It just makes everyone weaker.

So yeah, those words—fairness, belonging, community—they’re real to me because I’ve lived the good and the bad sides of them. I want people to feel they matter, that they can contribute, and that nobody gets left out just because of where they come from.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character17_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting in the garden, honestly, I feel a mix of things. Mostly, I feel curious and hopeful. Growing up, my street was always a mix—different races, families barely scraping by, some folks who just arrived in the country, and some who’d lived there forever. So, seeing all these different faces isn’t new for me. It’s kind of comforting, actually, because it reminds me of home. I like hearing different languages and seeing people celebrate their own traditions.

At the same time, I won’t pretend it’s always easy. Sometimes there’s awkwardness, especially if folks keep to themselves or if we just don’t understand each other’s ways. Like, I’ve seen neighbors get nervous around people who act differently—maybe someone’s drinking too much, or a family with strange customs. But I try to remind myself, everybody’s got their own struggles and stories. I’ve had neighbors who were judged just because they spoke Spanish or lived with a bunch of relatives, but when you talk to them, you realize they’re just trying to get by like anyone else.

Mostly, I want to reach out, say hi, ask about their day. You’d be surprised what happens when you just listen. Even if we don’t agree or our lives are totally different, I think it’s important to show respect. That’s how you build trust. If we all just sit in our corners, nothing changes. So I try to be open, even if it’s uncomfortable sometimes. I’d rather try and fail at connecting than not try at all. That’s how I see it.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
I’ll be real with you: in a neighborhood like ours, where folks come from all kinds of backgrounds and struggle with different things, the most important thing is not jumping to judge. I’ve seen neighbors shut people out because they drink too much, or because their family doesn’t “look right.” But if we want people to feel comfortable, you gotta start with respect. That means saying hello, even if you don’t agree with how someone lives. Sometimes people just need someone to see them—not just their problems.

I think we need more honest conversation. When folks feel nervous about someone with substance abuse or an infectious disease, usually it’s because they don’t know much. Instead of gossiping or avoiding them, why not ask, “Hey, are you okay? Need anything?” or learn a bit about what they’re going through. Same thing with people from other countries or who speak a different language—maybe try to learn a word or two, or just listen. You’d be surprised how much that means to someone who feels out of place.

Tolerance matters because if you start drawing lines—“we don’t talk to them,” or “I don’t want my kids around those people”—pretty soon everybody’s isolated. I’ve seen it: families who just keep to themselves because they’re scared of judgment, or people who get pushed away because others don’t understand their illness or lifestyle. That’s not how a neighborhood should be.

For me, being comfortable means knowing you won’t be shamed or ignored. We can set boundaries if someone’s behavior is dangerous, sure, but we should do it with care, not hate. And instead of whispering about someone, maybe ask them how you can help or what they need. More communication helps everyone realize we’re all human, with problems and strengths.

I’m always willing to talk about this, because I’ve lived it. I know how loneliness and judgment can hurt. I want a community where differences aren’t just tolerated but valued—where people feel safe to be themselves, and know someone will have their back, even if they mess up sometimes. That’s the kind of place I want to live in.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character17_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one, and I’ve thought about it a lot. When jobs are tight and money’s short, people get scared—worried about how they’ll feed their kids or pay rent. I get it; I’ve been there too. Fairness, to me, starts with making sure everyone has a chance to earn a living, especially those who’ve been in the community for a long time and have always contributed.

But I also know what it’s like to be seen as “the outsider.” My own family came here from Mexico, and I remember my parents struggling to find work, even when they’d do anything and work any hours. Migrant workers often take jobs most people don’t want, and they work hard. They’re here trying to build a better life, just like everyone else. I don’t think it’s fair to blame them for problems that are bigger than just who gets hired.

So, I think balance means two things. First, we need good protections for local workers—fair wages, rules against exploitation, chances for training and advancement. If you’re from here, you shouldn’t get pushed out by companies looking for cheaper labor. But second, we can’t shut the door on newcomers. Migrants bring a lot, and many businesses and families depend on them.

Maybe it means setting rules so everyone gets a fair shot: making sure employers aren’t underpaying people or ignoring labor laws just because someone’s new or desperate. Maybe it means supporting programs that help both locals and migrants get the skills they need. And we have to be honest—sometimes the real problem is companies taking advantage, not just workers competing against each other.

For me, fairness is about fighting for everyone’s dignity, not pitting people against each other. We need to make sure local families don’t get left behind, but also remember that migrant workers are part of our community too. If we treat each other with respect and fight for better conditions for all, that’s the only way things get better. Otherwise, we’re just fighting over scraps, and nobody wins.

What I'm proposing isn't open borders or fortress America. It's a managed system that recognizes both our national interests and our humanitarian values. That's the America I want to live in.

responses.answer:
Fairness, to me, has always been about who gets a seat at the table—and whether folks like us, the ones working two jobs just to keep the lights on, actually count when decisions are made. I don’t mean fairness like everybody wins a prize. I mean real fairness—like, if you’re doing the same work, living by the rules, paying taxes, why should someone get treated different just 'cause of where they came from or how they talk?

I remember growing up in East L.A., my mom cleaning houses five days a week, sometimes six. She didn’t complain much, but I saw it—the way some people looked at her, like she was invisible unless something needed fixing. That stuck with me. Fairness isn’t just laws on paper. It’s how you’re treated in the grocery line, at the clinic, when your kid’s teacher talks down to you. Belonging? That’s knowing you’re not just *allowed* here—you’re *wanted* here.

My abuela used to say, “La comunidad no es donde vives, es quien te espera cuando falta pan.” The community isn't where you live—it's who waits for you when there's no bread. That hit hard during the pandemic, when neighbors started leaving food on each other’s porches without even knocking. No grand speeches—just showing up. That’s belonging. Not papers, not accents, not how long you’ve been here. It’s about showing care when it matters.

And community… that’s not just a block party or a PTA meeting full of the same three people. Real community means looking out for the quiet guy down the hall who’s struggling with drink, or the new family from Guatemala who don’t know how to sign up for school meals. It means not turning away just because someone’s messy or scared or speaks broken English—because maybe once, we were that family too.

I think about my cousin Rico—he got picked up in a worksite raid back in ’08. Didn’t matter that he’d been here 15 years, building homes, sending his kids to Catholic school. One day gone. That tore something open in our family. Made me realize belonging can feel strong—until someone says, “You don’t belong,” and the system backs them up.

So yeah, fairness, belonging, community—they’re all tied. You can’t have one without the others. And when we talk about immigrants? I see my tías, my uncles, my own grandparents. I don’t see “others.” I see us.

Sitting here in the garden, hands in the dirt, I feel… at peace. This plot? It’s mine, but it’s everyone’s too. You see Ms. Lin from across the street tending her bitter melon vines like they’re family. Old Mr. Jenkins—white as milk and twice as sour sometimes—still waves, even if he mutters about “too many smells” from people’s cooking. (I laugh a little.) But you know what? Last week, he brought over a jar of pickled beets to the Somali woman on the corner—Ayan—who feeds half the block when she makes *canjeero*. He didn’t say much, just handed it over. She smiled like the sun came out.

That’s what this place is. Messy. Loud. Sometimes smelly. But real.

I watch the young couple two doors down—unmarried, both women, one Puerto Rican, one white girl from Ohio. They got side-eye when they first moved in, sure. But then they fixed Mrs. Gutierrez’s porch step after the storm, no asking for anything. Now people bring them cookies. That’s how it works around here—deeds matter more than labels.

And yeah, there’s folks struggling. Like Javier, who lives behind the bodega. Drinks too much, sleeps in his truck sometimes. People whisper. But I remember my uncle went through that after he lost his job at the plant. Nobody helped him then. So now? I make sure Javier gets an extra plate when we do community meals. Not because I’m saintly—but because shame don’t fix pain. Community does.

There’s a Haitian family three houses up. Just got here last year. Don’t speak much English. The kids are quiet in school, teachers say. But in this garden? Their little girl sings while she pulls weeds. In Kreyòl. And you know what? Half of us don’t understand a word—but we hum along anyway.

That’s belonging. Not perfect. Not easy. But present.

I used to think diversity meant just having different people around. Now I know—it means being willing to lean in when it’s uncomfortable. To sit with someone’s silence, their accent, their grief, their joy—even if it doesn’t look like yours.

This garden grows more than tomatoes. It grows patience. Grows respect. One seed at a time.

responses.answer:
Fairness, when jobs are tight? That’s not about who came first. It’s about who’s *here now* and how we treat each other when the pot’s not big enough.

Look—I’ve stood in line at temp agencies where they hand the work slips to guys with lighter skin first. I’ve seen bosses hire undocumented folks not because they’re “stealing” jobs, but because they’ll pay them less, no questions asked. That ain’t the workers’ fault. That’s greed. And it hurts all of us—citizens, legal residents, newcomers—because it drags wages down for everyone.

I remember working at that warehouse before my knee gave out. There was me, a few Black women from the neighborhood, some white guys laid off from the factory, and a handful of Guatemalan men who didn’t have papers. We all wanted the same thing: steady hours, enough to cover rent, maybe put something aside. But the boss played us against each other—“These guys don’t complain,” he’d say, or “At least you got an address, unlike them.” Divide and conquer. That’s not fair. That’s exploitation.

So fairness, to me, means no one gets thrown under the bus just because they’re more vulnerable. If jobs are scarce, then we fix the system—not scapegoat the people at the bottom.

That means enforcing labor laws equally. Pay minimum wage. Overtime. Safe conditions. No matter your accent, your status, your color. When you do that, you stop pitting poor against poor. Because then it’s not “me vs. the immigrant”—it’s *workers* vs. the boss who’s cheating us all.

And yeah, I get it—when someone’s been here their whole life, paying taxes, playing by the rules, it stings to see folks come in and—well, not follow the lines. But let’s be real: most of these migrant workers aren’t skipping queues for fun. They’re running from violence, drought, poverty our own government’s policies helped create south of the border. You think a mother walking through the desert with her baby’s doing it because she wants a free ride? She’s doing it because she’s out of options.

So balance? It’s not about choosing between “locals” and “migrants.” It’s about making sure both are protected. Prioritize hiring locally? Sure—if the job’s public, if it’s funded by our taxes. But don’t shut the door on newcomers trying to survive. Instead, expand opportunity. Push for job training, childcare, transit—things that help *all* of us move up.

And while we’re at it—stop blaming immigrants for broken systems. The hospital closing? Not because of Spanish speakers. The school overcrowding? Not because of refugee kids. It’s underfunding. It’s greed. It’s politicians cutting corners while telling us to fight each other.

True fairness means seeing that we’re in this together—whether born here or not. Because when one of us is exploited, it makes it easier to exploit the rest. But when we stand side by side—citizen, immigrant, documented, struggling—we got power.

I won’t turn my back on someone just because they crossed a line on a map. My abuela didn’t. And I won’t forget that.

I hear all these arguments—on the news, at the bus stop, in church hallways—and I try to listen, even when my gut tightens. Because people aren’t just throwing words around. They’re scared. Tired. Worried about their kids’ future. But fear don’t always tell the truth.

And cultural diversity? Walk through my neighborhood and you’ll smell it—tamales, jerk chicken, injera, halal beef. Kids code-switch between English, Spanglish, Arabic before lunch. That ain’t weakening us—it’s making us richer. More flavor. More music. More ways of seeing the world. When my niece learned how to say “thank you” in Somali from her classmate, something softened in me. Like we’re not so far apart after all.

But then there’s the fear talk—crime, terrorism, disease. That one gets under my skin. Not because it’s not felt—people *are* afraid—but because it’s twisted. I’ve lived in tough neighborhoods. Crime? Yeah, it happens. But it’s not because someone’s from Honduras. It’s because folks are poor, desperate, or broken by systems that never helped them. And linking immigrants to terrorism? Come on. That’s fear-mongering. I want safety too—I lock my door, I check my block. But I also know the guy from Yemen who runs the corner store sends money home to his sisters. He’s not a threat. He’s a man trying to live.

And let’s talk numbers. I’ve read studies—FBI, Bureau of Justice—undocumented immigrants commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born citizens. Lower! But you don’t hear that on TV. All you hear is one horror story blown up like a balloon. One bad apple don’t mean the whole orchard’s rotten.

Forgotten that?

And yes—some worry immigration pulls wages down or takes jobs. That fear? It’s not made up. I’ve seen it happen. When bosses hire off the books, pay cash, no benefits—that hurts all workers. But again, that’s not the immigrant’s fault. That’s the employer breaking the law. So why punish the vulnerable instead of holding the powerful accountable?

What needs more dialogue? The security stuff. Not because it’s not worth talking about—but because facts get drowned out by noise. People need real info, not slogans. Like: most refugees go through years of vetting. Or: public health services help everyone stay healthy—including us. We need town halls where nurses, cops, pastors, and immigrants sit together and talk without yelling. Where we ask, “What are you really afraid of?” and actually listen.

And income fears? Yeah. Let’s talk about that. But let’s also talk about raising the minimum wage. Fixing housing. Making healthcare affordable. Because if we solve those, we lift *everyone*—not by pushing others down, but by building a floor strong enough to hold us all.

So which views are reasonable? The ones rooted in dignity—the labor argument, the cultural joy, the humanitarian call. The ones that need more evidence and conversation? The fear-based ones—crime, terrorism, “they’re destroying our way of life.” Those need light. Need truth. Need neighbors talking, not politicians screaming.

Because at the end of the day, I don’t want a country that’s “safe” by being cold. I want one that’s strong because it’s fair. That’s what my abuela believed. That’s what I believe.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character17_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for complete openness—not because I don’t care, but because real life isn’t a dream. We’ve got schools that are already overcrowded, clinics with waitlists, rents climbing so fast even long-time folks are getting pushed out. So yeah, we need some structure. But “structure” shouldn’t mean cruelty.

What I’d want? A mix—something *practical*, but also *human*.

First: **admit people based on job demand**, but only if those jobs pay fair wages and protect workers. Not just any job—good ones. Because right now, “job-based” immigration too often means exploiting people in the shadows. No overtime. No safety gear. No voice. That hurts everyone. So tie it to labor standards. If a farm needs pickers, fine—but they’ve got to pay decently, offer clean water, let workers report abuse without fear. Same for nursing homes, construction, meatpacking. Make the employer follow the rules *first*. Then bring people in legally, safely.

Second: **set reasonable numerical limits**, not arbitrary caps designed to keep people out, but numbers based on what our communities can actually absorb—with support. Not just dumping families in cities with no housing or language help. Plan for it. Fund ESL programs. Expand affordable housing. Train caseworkers. I know that costs money—but so does chaos. And besides, immigrants pay taxes too. Let’s stop pretending they’re all leeching. They’re contributing—from day one.

But—and this is big—**create a real path to legal status for people already here**. The ones working, raising kids, going to church, paying rent. My neighbor Rosa—been here 18 years, owns a food truck, her kids are U.S. citizens. Still no papers. That don’t make sense. That ain’t fair. So regularize their status. Stop living in fear. Let them step into the light.

And humanitarian intake? **Keep doors open for refugees and asylum seekers**, especially from places torn apart by violence or climate disaster—places where U.S. policy helped make things worse. We’ve got a moral duty. And processing shouldn’t take years. Streamline it. Hire more judges. Treat people like humans, not case numbers.

But under no circumstances would I support **refusing entry to workers from other countries altogether**. That’s madness. Who’s gonna harvest our food? Care for our elders? Flip the burgers? And shutting the door completely? That’s not strength—that’s fear wearing a flag.

Fairness, to me, means no double standards. If you want someone to do hard work, you treat them right. If you say “we’re a nation of laws,” then *enforce* the laws fairly—for employers, for workers, for everyone. Not just the ones who can’t fight back.

And social integration? That doesn’t happen by keeping people afraid or invisible. It happens when kids go to school together. When neighbors share gardens. When people can speak their truth without being punished for their accent.

So my ideal policy?  
- **Merit + need + humanity.**  
- **Work visas tied to rights, not just labor.**  
- **A clear, reachable path to belonging.**  
- **Support for communities taking people in.**

Not perfect. But just. Not closed. Not chaotic. *Balanced.*

Because I want my niece to grow up in a country that’s strong not because it’s shut tight—but because it’s wide enough to hold both justice and mercy. That’s the America I believe in. That’s the one my family came for—even if they didn’t know it at the time.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character17_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character17_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did.

I didn’t expect it, but stepping into her voice—really trying to speak not just *for* her, but *as* her—brought something back. Not just memories, but the *weight* of how she saw things. Like, I remembered how she’d pause before speaking at community meetings, even though she had the clearest mind in the room. Not because she wasn’t sure—but because she knew people would dismiss her: too brown, too working-class, too “emotional.” But her emotion? That was wisdom. It came from living it.

While doing this, I realized something: Character17_F didn’t see immigration as a political issue first. She saw it as a *human chain*—one generation reaching back to pull the next forward. She never said “intersectionality,” but that’s what she lived. She connected the struggle of the queer teen kicked out by his family to the asylum seeker sleeping in a shelter because they both knew what it meant to be told, “You don’t belong.”

And honestly? I’ve always agreed with her on fairness, but I think I used to separate “us” and “them” a little more than she ever did. I worried more about resources. I listened too much to the fear—the “what if there’s not enough?” But embodying her reminded me: scarcity is often manufactured. The real lack isn’t jobs or housing—it’s courage. Courage to share, to organize, to demand better from those in power instead of blaming the ones beside us.

She wouldn’t have wanted walls—literal or in our heads. She’d want strong communities where everyone has a shot, no matter where they started. And she’d remind us that belonging isn’t earned. It’s claimed—by showing up, by caring, by refusing to let anyone eat alone.

This made me feel closer to her. Like she’s not just gone—she’s still teaching. Still pushing. And maybe that’s the point of conversations like this: not just to remember someone, but to let them keep changing you.

So thank you—for asking me to do this. For keeping her voice alive. Because we still need it. Now more than ever.
